strengths: The orientation-resolved heatmaps reveal useful structure in generalization that aggregate accuracy obscures. The distinction between local rotations, in-plane rotations, and poorly generalized viewpoints should interest researchers studying visual robustness and learned representations.

The behavioral evidence spans three object categories, multiple seed-orientation distributions, three network architectures, pretraining, augmentation, and cross-category transfer. Keeping training-set size fixed and repeating experiments with five randomized instance assignments strengthens the diversity comparisons.

The geometric model offers an interpretable descriptive account, with high reported correlations and informative component ablations. The learning paradigm and visual examples communicate the central behavioral finding clearly, and the manuscript provides a public data/code link.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central mechanistic claims exceed the evidence. Figure 4 shows activation examples and correlations, but does not establish that shared, discriminative features causally transmit orientation invariance from fully-seen to partially-seen objects. Common orientation-dependent image statistics could also produce similar responses. Targeted neuron or feature interventions could support the stronger interpretation; otherwise, the abstract and discussion should consistently describe a supported hypothesis. The conclusion that biological recognition mechanisms largely apply to DNNs also requires qualification.

Necessary: Section 4.2 fits the geometric model by optimizing Pearson correlation with network accuracy, but describes no held-out evaluation of that fit. Consequently, the reported correlations support descriptive agreement, while independent predictive validity remains unestablished. Report an appropriate fitting/evaluation separation or narrow the predictive claims. Furthermore, Section 4.3 defines generalizable orientations using 10% of this fitted model's maximum. Pearson fitting does not calibrate output levels, so this cutoff needs justification and sensitivity analysis before supporting subsequent partition-based conclusions.

Necessary: The invariance measure needs validation against alternative explanations. Equations 5–7 compare region-averaged activations; equal means can conceal strongly orientation-dependent responses. The activity filter additionally retains only neuron–instance pairs active in both regions, excluding seed-active neurons that lose their response at unseen orientations. This selection can bias the summary toward invariance. Analyses using orientation-level responses and units selected independently of their OoD responses, together with threshold sensitivity, are needed to substantiate the neuronal interpretation.

Necessary: Important evaluation and statistical details remain unclear. Specify independent evaluation-image generation, per-orientation sample counts, the orientation-grid resolution, and whether OoD-based learning-rate selection used separate validation data. Define the error bars and report quantitative neural correlations with their sampling units and uncertainty. Figure 4's text alternately describes points as instances and orientations, while the equations average over both neurons and instances, making the plotted aggregation difficult to reconstruct.

Optional: Larger labels in the dense quantitative figures would improve usability. Reporting Haar-weighted orientation averages would also clarify sensitivity to viewpoint weighting, since independent uniform Euler-angle sampling is not uniform over SO(3). Broader rendering conditions would extend the findings, but are unnecessary if conclusions remain scoped to the tested setting.
